i-thought-i-understood-node-modules-then.html:
The question that started it

I have typed npm install more times than I can count. A folder called node_modules appears, my app runs, and I move on. Then I stumbled across pnpm, and one claim stopped me: it can install packages without copying them.

That made me curious about what really happens on disk during an install. Where do the files go? Why does every project carry its own heavy copy of the same libraries? And how could anything install without copying?

So I went down the rabbit hole. This article is what I found, in the order I found it: one "wait, really?" at a time.

First, what npm does

npm builds a flat, hoisted node_modules. Since npm v3 it pulls almost every dependency, including the dependencies of your dependencies, up to the top level, because Node finds packages by walking up the directory tree.

node_modules/
├── express/
├── body-parser/      <- not mine, but hoisted to the top
├── debug/            <- same
└── ...

It is simple and it works. But once I looked closely, four side effects jumped out:

  • Full copies everywhere. Every project extracts its own copy of every package. npm does keep a cache in ~/.npm/_cacache, but it holds tarballs, so each install still unpacks fresh files. Ten projects using lodash means ten copies of lodash on disk.

  • Phantom dependencies. Because body-parser is hoisted, I can require('body-parser') without ever declaring it. It works today. It breaks the day an update shuffles the hoisting.

  • Doppelgangers. If two packages need different versions of the same dependency, one version takes the top-level slot and the other gets nested. The same package can end up duplicated in several places.

  • A layout that is a result, not a rule. Even with package-lock.json, the tree's shape comes out of an algorithm. Nothing in the structure itself guarantees it.

The phantom dependency one bothered me most. It means my package.json can quietly lie about what my code needs.

Then I met pnpm: three ideas that make it work

pnpm answers the "how can it install without copying?" question with three mechanisms that work together.

Idea 1: a store that knows files by their contents

pnpm keeps one store per machine. Files in it are named by the hash of their contents, not by the package they came from. A package is unpacked into the store once, no matter how many projects use it.

The part that made me stop: this is file-level, not package-level. If foo@1.0.0 and foo@1.0.1 differ in only two files, pnpm stores only those two new files. Everything unchanged is shared between versions.

Idea 2: hard links instead of copies

When I install, pnpm does not copy files out of the store. It hard-links them into my project. A hard link is a second directory entry pointing at the same bytes on disk, so the file exists once and appears in two places. On filesystems with copy-on-write support, such as APFS and Btrfs, pnpm can use reflinks instead. If the store and the project sit on different filesystems, it falls back to plain copying.

Idea 3: symlinks that rebuild the dependency graph

Hard links solve storage. They do not solve how Node finds packages. That is where the symlinks come in:

my-project/
└── node_modules/
    ├── express -> .pnpm/express@4.18.2/node_modules/express
    └── .pnpm/
        ├── express@4.18.2/
        │   └── node_modules/
        │       ├── express/        <- hard-linked from the store
        │       ├── body-parser -> ../../body-parser@1.20.1/node_modules/body-parser
        │       └── debug       -> ../../debug@2.6.9/node_modules/debug
        ├── body-parser@1.20.1/
        └── debug@2.6.9/

Reading this tree makes the design clear:

  • The top-level node_modules holds only what I declared in package.json, as symlinks.

  • .pnpm/ is a virtual store with one folder per name@version.

  • Inside each package's folder, its own dependencies sit next to it as siblings.

So pnpm is not inventing a new way to find packages. It arranges the files so that the way Node already works gives the right answer.

So why does it feel faster?

Understanding the store takes the magic out of the speed claim. It comes down to how much work happens per file.

npm

pnpm

Work per file on a warm install

Extract from tarball, write to disk

Hard link a file that already exists in the store

Reuse across projects

Tarball cache only

Disk usage

Grows with every project

One copy plus links

Creating a link is a metadata operation. Writing a file is real I/O. When the store already has what a project needs, pnpm mostly skips the writing. It also overlaps resolving, fetching and linking per package, rather than finishing one stage before starting the next.

Here is the honest part, and I want to be clear about it. A cold install, with an empty store or cache, is limited by the network, so the gap shrinks a lot. The advantage shows up on repeat installs, in CI with a cached store, and in monorepos. npm has also improved over the years, so published benchmark numbers vary by version, project and machine. I would treat any "X times faster" headline as a hypothesis, and I plan to test it on my own projects.

The side effect I liked most: strictness

Because my top-level node_modules contains only declared dependencies, require('body-parser') from my own code simply fails if I never listed it. The phantom dependency problem from earlier does not resolve, by design.

Trace what happens when Express itself asks for body-parser:

  1. Node follows the express symlink to its real path, .pnpm/express@4.18.2/node_modules/express.

  2. It looks in the parent node_modules folder.

  3. body-parser is sitting right there, as a symlink to its own folder in the virtual store.

No custom resolver, no patched require. Each package sees exactly the dependencies it declared, and my code sees exactly mine. A strict dependency graph, built out of plain symlinks and standard Node behaviour.

In npm's world, package.json is a suggestion that the folder layout may or may not honour. In pnpm's world, it is enforced.

The rabbit hole kept going

The architecture was the headline, but pnpm has more under the hood. These are the features I bookmarked to try:

  • Workspaces for monorepos. A pnpm-workspace.yaml file defines the packages. The workspace: protocol (for example "my-lib": "workspace:*") links local packages together and is rewritten to a real version on publish.

  • Filtering. pnpm --filter ./apps/web... build builds one app plus everything it depends on, and --filter "...[origin/main]" runs a command only on packages changed since main.

  • Catalogs. Define a dependency version once in the workspace file and reference it from many packages with catalog:, so a monorepo stays consistent.

  • Native patching. pnpm patch and pnpm patch-commit maintain fixes to third-party packages without a separate tool.

  • Safer install scripts. In recent major versions, pnpm does not run dependency lifecycle scripts such as postinstall by default. You explicitly allow the packages you trust, which closes off a common supply-chain attack route. The exact setting names have been evolving, so I would check the docs for the version I install.

  • Docker and CI helpers. pnpm fetch fills the store from the lockfile alone, which suits Docker layer caching, and pnpm deploy produces a pruned, self-contained copy of one workspace package.

  • Housekeeping. pnpm dlx works like npx, and pnpm store prune removes packages nothing uses any more.

The lockfile is pnpm-lock.yaml, one file for the whole workspace and designed to be friendlier to merge conflicts.

Where it gets awkward

I did not want to write a love letter, so here is what I expect to bite.

Tools that assume a flat layout. Some older libraries and certain bundler, React Native or Electron setups reach for packages they never declared. Under pnpm's strict layout they fail. There are three escape hatches, from gentle to blunt:

  1. public-hoist-pattern hoists specific packages to the top level.

  2. shamefully-hoist=true hoists everything, npm-style.

  3. node-linker=hoisted drops the symlink structure entirely.

The filesystem gotcha. Hard links only work within one filesystem. If the store and the project live on different ones, which can happen with some Docker bind mounts and CI cache layers, pnpm quietly falls back to copying. The install still works, but the speed and disk savings disappear.

A new mental model. node_modules is no longer a plain tree of folders. Debugging it means following symlinks, and that will feel unfamiliar for a while.

None of these are dealbreakers. They are the price of the strictness, and the strictness is the point.

What I am going to try next

Reading about hard links is one thing. I want to see them. My plan:

  1. Catch the hard links in the act. Install the same package in two projects, then compare inode numbers of the same file. If pnpm's story holds, both paths should show one identical number.

  2. Measure it myself. Migrate one side project from npm to pnpm and compare warm install time and disk usage, instead of trusting someone else's benchmark.

  3. Break something on purpose. Find a dependency that relies on a phantom import and watch the strict layout reject it.

  4. Try a small monorepo. Set up a pnpm workspace with workspace: links, --filter, and a catalog.

  5. Test it in CI. Run it with a cached store, and check that the store and project share a filesystem so hard links do not turn into copies.

ls -li node_modules/.pnpm/<package>@<version>/node_modules/<package>/index.js

If the number in the first column matches across projects, the file really exists once.

I will write up what I find, including whatever breaks. If you have already made the switch from npm to pnpm, I would love to hear what surprised you, and which gotchas I should expect.

adding-sqs-and-idempotency-to-our-lambda.html:
Our profile picture service from AWS Lambda, Explained by Actually Building Something works, but it quietly assumes two things that production never grants: that traffic arrives politely, and that every upload triggers Lambda exactly once. In this follow-up we add an SQS queue between S3 and Lambda to absorb bursts, and an idempotency ledger in DynamoDB so a duplicate delivery does no harm.

The new architecture

Uploads land in S3, S3 hands each event to SQS, and Lambda drains the queue at its own pace. A message that fails five times moves to the dead-letter queue, and the DynamoDB ledger decides whether an upload was already handled.

Why the direct trigger breaks under real traffic

In the original design, S3 invokes Lambda directly for every uploaded picture. That is perfect for a demo and fragile at scale, for three reasons.

  • Bursts have nowhere to wait. If a campus-wide signup sends thousands of uploads in a minute, Lambda scales out to match, and everything downstream (your database, a third-party API, your account concurrency limit) takes the hit at once.

  • Failures are easy to lose. Asynchronous Lambda invocations are retried a limited number of times, and an event that keeps failing is dropped unless you configure a destination for it.

  • Duplicates are possible. S3 event notifications are delivered at least once, and Lambda retries make a second run of the same work even more likely.

A queue fixes the first two. The third needs a different tool, which is idempotency.

Putting SQS between S3 and Lambda

S3 now sends its event notification to an SQS standard queue, and Lambda reads from that queue through an event source mapping. The queue becomes a buffer: uploads can spike, but Lambda pulls work at a pace you control. Note that S3 can only notify standard queues, not FIFO queues, so duplicates remain possible even with a queue in the middle.

The queue

The queue is the shock absorber. Its most important setting is the visibility timeout: how long a message stays hidden after Lambda picks it up. If that is shorter than the function needs to finish, SQS assumes the work failed and hands the message out again while the first copy is still running. AWS recommends at least six times the function timeout.

The dead-letter queue

A second queue receives any message that fails too many times. Five attempts is a sensible start. It keeps one broken file from blocking healthy traffic, and it keeps the evidence for you to inspect, so give it a longer retention period than the main queue.

Batching and concurrency

Lambda pulls messages in small batches. Small batches limit the damage of one bad image, and a concurrency cap protects whatever sits downstream from a burst. Ask Lambda to report failures per message, so only the failed ones return to the queue.

One trap to avoid

Keep thumbnails in a different folder or bucket from the originals. If the function writes into the location that triggers it, every thumbnail triggers another run and the system feeds itself forever.

Why duplicates are unavoidable

SQS standard queues deliver each message at least once, which means the same message can occasionally arrive twice. Add S3's own at-least-once notifications, a Lambda timeout that lets the visibility window expire mid-work, and a retry after a partial batch failure, and the same upload can reach your code several times.

An operation is idempotent when running it twice leaves the system in the same state as running it once. For a resize job that is nearly free, because writing the same thumbnail to the same key twice changes nothing. It stops being free the moment the job also sends a welcome email, increments a counter or charges a fee.

So we use two layers:

  1. Deterministic outputs. Thumbnails always go to the same key, processed/<size>/<user-id>.jpg, so a repeat simply overwrites.

  2. A ledger of completed work. Before doing anything with side effects, the function checks a DynamoDB table to see whether this exact upload was already handled.

The ledger key must identify the upload, not the message. A message ID changes between deliveries, so it would never catch a duplicate. We use the bucket, the object key and the object's ETag together. If a user uploads a new photo to the same key, the ETag changes and the new photo is processed. If the same event arrives twice, the ETag matches and the second run is skipped.

How a ledger of completed work stops repeats

The idea is simple: before doing any work, check a small table that records which uploads are already handled. DynamoDB suits this because a conditional write lets only one caller create a given record, so two copies of the function cannot both claim the same upload.

Claiming the work

Each record is in one of two states. In progress means a copy of the function has claimed the upload and holds a time-limited lock. Completed means the work is done and later copies can skip it. The lock expires on its own, so a function that crashes mid-job does not block that upload forever.

Three possible outcomes

When a message arrives, the function finds one of three situations. Nobody has touched the upload, so it claims it and does the work. The upload is already completed, so it exits quietly and the message is deleted. Another copy is working on it right now, so it fails the message on purpose and SQS redelivers it later.

Cleaning up

Records carry an expiry time, and DynamoDB's time-to-live feature removes them automatically, so the table never grows without bound.

What it cannot promise

This gives effectively-once processing, not exactly-once. If a function crashes after a side effect but before marking the upload completed, the lock expires and the work runs again. That is why the first layer matters: make the side effects themselves safe to repeat, or pass your own idempotency key to any service you call.

Handling failures one message at a time

Each SQS message wraps an S3 event, so the function unwraps one, then the other, and runs every upload through the ledger steps above. S3 also sends a one-off test message when notifications are first configured, which the function should ignore.

Partial failures

If one message in a batch fails, the function reports just that message back to Lambda. The others are deleted from the queue as successes. Without this, one bad image would drag the whole batch back and cause needless duplicates.

Safe replays

Because the ledger skips completed uploads, retries and replays from the dead-letter queue are harmless. If a message holds several uploads and the second fails, the first is simply skipped the next time around.

Libraries

Powertools for AWS Lambda ships an idempotency utility and a batch processor that implement these same ideas, so you rarely need to build them by hand.

Poison messages, the DLQ and what to monitor

Some messages will never succeed: a corrupt file, a PNG renamed to .jpg, an object deleted before the function reached it. Without a limit, such a message would cycle through the queue forever. With maxReceiveCount set to 5, SQS moves it to the DLQ after five failed attempts, and the healthy traffic keeps flowing.

A DLQ only helps if someone looks at it. Set a CloudWatch alarm on the DLQ's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric so that a single stuck message pages a human. Once you have fixed the bug, SQS can redrive the messages from the DLQ back to the main queue, and the ledger makes that replay safe.

These are the metrics worth a dashboard:

  • Queue age. ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage on the main queue shows whether Lambda is keeping up. A growing value means you need more concurrency or faster code.

  • DLQ depth. Anything above zero deserves attention.

  • Throttles and errors. Lambda's own Throttles and Errors metrics tell you whether the concurrency cap is too tight.

  • Skipped duplicates. Count the "Skipping duplicate" log lines. A steady trickle is normal and healthy. A sudden jump suggests a visibility timeout that is too short.

Takeaways

A direct S3-to-Lambda trigger is a good way to learn, and a queue and a ledger are what make it safe to run for real.

  • SQS absorbs bursts, retries failures and gives bad messages a place to land, so one problem upload never blocks the rest.

  • Set the visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout, and always attach a DLQ.

  • Assume every message can arrive twice. Key your ledger on the upload (bucket, key, ETag), never on the message ID.

  • Use a conditional write in DynamoDB to claim work, and a TTL to clean up after yourself.

  • Make the side effects themselves repeat-safe wherever you can. The ledger gives effectively-once processing, not a guarantee of exactly-once.

  • Report failures per message so a single bad record does not drag a whole batch back into the queue.

If you built the original service, the changes are small: one queue, one DLQ, one table and about sixty lines of code. The result is a pipeline that stays calm when traffic spikes and when AWS delivers the same event twice.

aws-lambda-explained-by-actually-buildin.html:
Most Lambda tutorials do one of two things. They either give you a "Hello World" that returns a JSON string and call it a day, or they bury you in a metaphor of 3,000 words.

Let's do neither. We're going to build one real thing — a profile picture upload service — and every Lambda concept will show up on its own, in the order you'd actually trip over it.

By the end you'll understand cold starts, concurrency, retries, permissions, and why your function mysteriously ran twice.

First, what Lambda actually is

You give AWS a function. AWS runs it when something happens. You pay for the milliseconds it ran.

That's it. There's no server you SSH into, no process you keep alive, no systemctl restart at 2 AM. When nothing is happening, nothing is running, and nothing is being billed.

The trade is that you give up control. You can't keep a process alive between requests. You can't hold things in memory reliably. You can't run for more than 15 minutes. Whether that trade is worth it depends entirely on what you're building — we'll get to when it isn't worth it at the end.

The thing we're building

A user in your mobile app uploads a profile picture. You need to:

  1. Accept the upload

  2. Resize it into a thumbnail

  3. Strip the EXIF data (because photos carry GPS coordinates and your users would rather you didn't publish those)

  4. Save the thumbnail

  5. Update the user's record with the new URL

On a traditional server, this is a route handler. On Lambda, it's going to become three or four functions and a queue, and by the time we're done you'll see exactly why.

Let's start with the naive version.

Your first function

Here's the whole thing:

import json

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    print("something happened")
    return {
        "statusCode": 200,
        "body": json.dumps({"ok": True})
    }

Three things to notice.

lambda_handler is just a name. You configure which function AWS should call — the default is filename.function_name, so lambda_function.lambda_handler. Nothing magic about it.

event is the input. It's a dict (or JSON object, depending on your runtime) and its shape depends entirely on what triggered you. An S3 event looks nothing like an API Gateway event, which looks nothing like an SQS event. This is the single most common source of confusion for beginners — there's no universal event schema. Print it once and look at it.

context is metadata about this invocation. Request ID, how many milliseconds you have left before timeout, memory limit, log stream name. Most people ignore it. The useful one is context.get_remaining_time_in_millis(), which we'll actually use later.

The return value matters only when someone's listening. For API Gateway it becomes the HTTP response. For S3 events, nobody reads it and you can return None.

What happens when this runs

Here's the part that explains basically every weird Lambda behavior you'll encounter.

When an invocation arrives and there's no environment available, AWS:

  1. Provisions a micro-VM (Firecracker, if you're curious)

  2. Downloads your code

  3. Starts the language runtime

  4. Runs everything at the top of your file — imports, global variables, module-level code

  5. Calls your handler

Steps 1–4 are the init phase. Step 5 is the invoke phase.

That init phase is the cold start. It's the reason your first request takes 800ms and the next one takes 40ms.

But here's the important part: the environment stays alive afterward. AWS keeps it around for a while — could be minutes, could be longer, it's not documented and you shouldn't depend on the number. If another request arrives during that window, AWS skips straight to step 5.

Which leads directly to the single best optimization in Lambda:

import boto3
from PIL import Image

# This runs ONCE per environment, not once per request
s3 = boto3.client("s3")
dynamodb = boto3.resource("dynamodb")
table = dynamodb.Table("users")

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    # This runs on every request
    ...

Anything expensive that can be reused — SDK clients, database connection pools, loaded config, a compiled regex — belongs outside the handler. Creating a boto3 client takes real time. Do it once and every warm invocation gets it free.

The flip side is the trap: anything you put in global scope persists between requests. Including mistakes.

# DON'T DO THIS
processed_users = []

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    processed_users.append(event["user_id"])   # grows forever
    return {"count": len(processed_users)}

That list survives across invocations in the same environment. Your count will be wrong, it'll be differently wrong depending on which environment handled the request, and it'll reset at random when AWS recycles things. Treat global scope as read-only cache, never as storage.

Cold starts, honestly

People panic about cold starts more than they need to. Some real context:

  • A small Python or Node function: roughly 100–400ms of init.

  • A function with heavy imports (pandas, a big SDK, anything that loads at import time): 1–3 seconds, easily.

  • A Java or .NET function without tuning: worse.

  • Attached to a VPC: this used to be brutal (10+ seconds). AWS fixed it years ago and it's now a small addition, not a disaster. Old blog posts will scare you about this — ignore them.

When does it matter? Only on user-facing synchronous paths. If your Lambda is processing a queue in the background, nobody cares that one message took an extra 400ms.

What actually helps:

Import less. from PIL import Image is cheaper than importing a library that pulls in half of scipy. Check what you actually need.

Import lazily if a heavy dependency is only needed on some code paths:

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    if event.get("needs_pdf"):
        import heavy_pdf_library   # only pay for it when you use it

Give it more memory (more on why below — it also gets you more CPU, which speeds up init).

Provisioned concurrency if you genuinely need consistent low latency. You tell AWS to keep N environments warm and initialized. It costs money whether or not they're used, which somewhat undermines the whole point of serverless, but it's there when latency actually matters.

The old trick of pinging your function every 5 minutes to keep it warm does work, but only keeps one environment warm. The moment you get two concurrent requests, one of them is cold anyway.

The memory setting is actually a CPU setting

This is the most underrated knob in Lambda and almost nobody touches it.

You configure memory from 128 MB to 10,240 MB. What AWS doesn't put in bold is that CPU scales proportionally with memory. At around 1,769 MB you get one full vCPU. Below that you get a fraction. Above that, more.

So for our image resizing function — which is CPU-bound, not memory-bound — bumping memory from 128 MB to 1024 MB doesn't just give it more room. It makes it roughly 8× faster.

And here's the counterintuitive bit: that can make it cheaper. You're billed for GB-seconds. If you double the memory but the function finishes in a third of the time, you just cut your bill.

128 MB  × 3000 ms = 384 MB-seconds
1024 MB ×  380 ms = 389 MB-seconds   ← same cost, 8× faster

The default of 128 MB is a terrible default for anything doing real work. Test your function at a few memory settings and look at the actual billed duration. AWS Lambda Power Tuning is an open-source tool that automates exactly this, and it's worth the twenty minutes.

Timeouts

Default is 3 seconds. Maximum is 15 minutes.

Three seconds catches a lot of people, because everything works fine in testing and then one slow third-party API call blows past it in production.

When the timeout hits, your function is killed. Not gracefully — no cleanup, no finally block, no chance to log what happened. You just see a timeout in CloudWatch and get to guess.

Two practical habits:

Set your timeout slightly above your realistic worst case, not at the max. A function that's supposed to take 2 seconds shouldn't have a 15-minute timeout — that just means a hung network call burns 15 minutes of billing before anyone notices.

Set your HTTP client timeouts below your Lambda timeout. If your function has 10 seconds and your API call has no timeout configured, you'll get killed mid-call with no error message. If the call times out at 8 seconds, you get a real exception you can log and handle.

You can also use the context object to bail out cleanly:

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    for item in items:
        if context.get_remaining_time_in_millis() < 2000:
            # save progress, exit cleanly instead of being murdered
            checkpoint(item)
            break
        process(item)

Statelessness and the one place you can write

You get a writable /tmp directory — 512 MB by default, configurable up to 10 GB. Use it for temporary work:

import os

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    local_path = f"/tmp/{event['key']}"
    s3.download_file(bucket, event["key"], local_path)
    thumbnail = resize(local_path)
    s3.upload_file(thumbnail, output_bucket, f"thumbs/{event['key']}")
    os.remove(local_path)   # clean up — /tmp persists between warm invocations too

Note that last line. /tmp survives across warm invocations in the same environment, so if you write 200 MB per request and never delete it, you'll eventually get "no space left on device" errors on a function that worked fine yesterday. That's a genuinely confusing bug the first time you hit it.

Everything that needs to actually persist goes to S3, DynamoDB, RDS, wherever. The environment is disposable and you should assume it disappears the instant your handler returns.

How your function gets invoked (and why it changes everything)

This is the part that most tutorials skip and it determines how failures behave.

There are three invocation models.

Synchronous

The caller waits for your response. API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, a direct SDK call.

If your function throws an exception, the caller gets the error immediately. AWS does not retry. Retrying is the caller's problem.

Client → API Gateway → Lambda → response

Asynchronous

The caller drops an event and leaves. S3 notifications, EventBridge, SNS.

AWS accepts the event, queues it internally, and invokes you. The caller already got its "202 Accepted" and is long gone.

If your function fails, AWS retries — twice, with delays. You didn't ask for this and you can't easily turn it off (you can set retry attempts to 0, but the default is 2). After the retries, the event goes to your configured dead-letter queue or on-failure destination. If you didn't configure one, it's gone forever.

S3 upload → (AWS queue) → Lambda
                             ↓ fails
                          retry, retry
                             ↓
                            DLQ

Poll-based

Lambda polls a source on your behalf. SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, MSK.

You don't get invoked by the source — Lambda's own service reads from the queue in batches and hands you the batch. This means retry behavior comes from the source, not from Lambda. For SQS, a failed batch becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and gets redelivered until it hits the queue's maxReceiveCount, at which point SQS moves it to the DLQ.

SQS ← Lambda service polls
       ↓
    your function (batch of up to 10 messages)

Why this matters: "how do I handle failures in Lambda" has three different answers depending on which of these you're using. A lot of confusing advice online is really just people answering for a different model than the one you're on.

Back to our upload service

Naive version: API Gateway → Lambda that does everything.

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    image = decode_base64(event["body"])
    save_original(image)
    thumb = resize(image)          # 2-4 seconds for a big photo
    strip_exif(thumb)
    upload_to_s3(thumb)
    update_user_record(thumb_url)  # database write
    return {"statusCode": 200, ...}

This works. It also means the user's phone holds an HTTP connection open for four seconds while their photo gets processed, and if anything in the middle fails, they get a 500 and the whole thing has to start over — including the upload.

Better version: split the fast part from the slow part.

Client
  ↓
API Gateway
  ↓
Lambda (presign)  →  returns an S3 upload URL, ~50ms
  ↓
Client uploads directly to S3
  ↓
S3 event notification (async)
  ↓
Lambda (process)  →  resize, strip EXIF, save
  ↓
DynamoDB

Now the API call is fast because it does almost nothing — it generates a pre-signed S3 URL and returns. The client uploads straight to S3, which is what S3 is good at. The heavy processing happens asynchronously, triggered by the upload itself. The user's request finished ages ago.

This pattern — do the minimum synchronously, push the real work to an async trigger — is most of what "designing for Lambda" actually means.

The bug you will definitely hit: it ran twice

Your processing Lambda resizes the image, uploads the thumbnail, updates DynamoDB — and then the DynamoDB write times out. The function throws. AWS retries. The image gets resized and uploaded again.

If your function also, say, charges a credit card or sends a welcome email, you now have a real problem.

Lambda guarantees at least once delivery for async and poll-based invocations. Not exactly once. Your code has to handle being run twice with the same input.

The fix is idempotency — making a repeated operation produce the same result as a single one.

Sometimes it's free. Writing to s3://thumbs/user-123.jpg twice just overwrites the same object. No harm.

Sometimes it isn't, and you need to track it:

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    request_id = event["Records"][0]["messageId"]   # stable across retries

    try:
        table.put_item(
            Item={"id": request_id, "status": "processing"},
            ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(id)"
        )
    except table.meta.client.exceptions.ConditionalCheckFailedException:
        print(f"{request_id} already handled, skipping")
        return

    do_the_actual_work(event)

The conditional write is the key — it's atomic, so two concurrent retries can't both win the race. Add a TTL on that table so the records clean themselves up.

One important detail: use an ID that's stable across retries. context.aws_request_id changes on every retry, so it's useless for this. The SQS messageId, the S3 object key + version, or an idempotency key your client generates — those work.

Concurrency, and the way Lambda kills your database

Lambda scales by running more copies of your function at the same time. One environment handles exactly one request at a time — there's no threading model where a single environment serves ten concurrent requests. Ten concurrent requests means ten environments.

Your account has a default concurrent execution limit (commonly 1,000, varies by region and account). That's shared across every function in the account and region.

Which sets up the classic serverless failure:

1000 concurrent Lambdas
        ↓
each opens a database connection
        ↓
Postgres with max_connections = 100
        ↓
"FATAL: sorry, too many clients already"

Your compute layer scaled beautifully. Your database did not. And then it fell over and took down your other services too.

Three things to know here:

Reserved concurrency caps a function. Set your database-touching function to 50 and it will never open more than 50 connections — extra invocations get throttled instead. Throttled synchronous calls return an error; throttled async calls get retried automatically, which is usually what you want.

RDS Proxy sits between Lambda and your relational database and pools connections, so 500 Lambdas share a small number of real connections. If you're using Lambda with RDS at any scale, you probably want this.

DynamoDB doesn't have this problem, which is a real part of why it shows up in every serverless architecture. It's HTTP-based with no connection state.

There's also a scaling rate limit, not just a ceiling — Lambda adds concurrency in bursts and then ramps. A sudden spike from 0 to 3,000 doesn't get 3,000 environments instantly. For spiky traffic, a queue in front absorbs the difference.

Permissions

Two separate things that get confused constantly.

The execution role is what your function can do. It's an IAM role your function assumes when it runs. Our processing function needs to read from one S3 bucket, write to another, and update one DynamoDB table:

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::uploads-bucket/*"
},
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["s3:PutObject"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::thumbnails-bucket/*"
},
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["dynamodb:UpdateItem"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:123456789:table/users"
}

Note what's not there: s3:* on *. It's genuinely tempting to write that when you're debugging at 11 PM, and it's how a compromised dependency in one small function ends up with read access to every bucket you own.

The resource policy is who can invoke your function. When you wire up an S3 trigger in the console, AWS quietly adds one of these allowing S3 to invoke you. This is why manually-created triggers sometimes don't fire — the permission's missing and the error is nowhere obvious.

Your function also needs logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, and logs:PutLogEvents, or you get no logs at all and debugging becomes archaeology. The AWS-managed AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole policy covers it.

Config and secrets

Environment variables are the normal way to pass configuration:

import os

TABLE_NAME = os.environ["USERS_TABLE"]
THUMBNAIL_BUCKET = os.environ["THUMBNAIL_BUCKET"]

Read them at module level so you fail fast on a misconfigured deploy rather than on the first request.

They're encrypted at rest, but they're visible in plaintext to anyone with console access to the function. Which makes them fine for a table name or a log level, and not fine for a database password.

For actual secrets, use Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store, and fetch at init:

import boto3, json

# init phase — runs once per environment
_secrets = boto3.client("secretsmanager")
DB_PASSWORD = json.loads(
    _secrets.get_secret_value(SecretId="prod/db")["SecretString"]
)["password"]

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    ...

Fetching at init means one API call per environment instead of one per request. Just be aware it adds to your cold start, and that rotated secrets won't be picked up until environments recycle.

Getting your code up there

Zip file. Your code and dependencies, up to 50 MB zipped / 250 MB unzipped. Fine for most things. Annoying the first time you discover that a library with C extensions compiled on your Mac doesn't run on Lambda's Linux — you need to build for the right platform.

Layers. A separate zip, up to five per function, shared across functions. Good for a dependency set that several functions share, or for keeping your deployment package small so you can still edit code in the console. The catch is that layers get their own versioning, and figuring out which function has which layer version six months later is not fun. Use them when there's a real reason.

Container images. Up to 10 GB. This is the answer when your dependencies are huge — anything ML-adjacent, ffmpeg, headless Chrome. You build a normal Docker image against an AWS base image and push it to ECR. Cold starts are surprisingly good because AWS caches layers aggressively.

For our image processing function, Pillow with its binary dependencies is exactly the case where you either use a prebuilt layer or just go with a container image.

Seeing what's going on

print() goes to CloudWatch Logs. That's the baseline and it works.

Do yourself a favor and log structured JSON instead of prose:

import json

def log(**kwargs):
    print(json.dumps(kwargs))

log(event="thumbnail_created", user_id=user_id, duration_ms=elapsed, size_bytes=size)

Because then CloudWatch Logs Insights can actually query it, and "show me every request over 3 seconds yesterday" becomes a query instead of a grep.

The metrics worth putting on a dashboard:

  • Errors and Throttles — the two that mean something is actively broken

  • Duration at p99, not average. Averages hide cold starts and the one pathological request.

  • ConcurrentExecutions — how close you are to the ceiling

  • IteratorAge for stream sources — if this is climbing, you're falling behind and will eventually lose data

  • DLQ depth — should be zero. If it isn't, something has been quietly failing.

And turn on X-Ray when you have more than two components. Once a request goes API Gateway → Lambda → SQS → Lambda → DynamoDB, "which hop was slow" is not a question you can answer from logs alone.

What this actually costs

The free tier is 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds per month, and it doesn't expire. Past that, roughly $0.20 per million requests plus about $0.0000166667 per GB-second.

Concretely, our thumbnail function at 1024 MB running 400ms, called 100,000 times a month:

Requests:  100,000 × $0.0000002        = $0.02
Compute:   100,000 × 0.4s × 1GB
           = 40,000 GB-seconds          = $0.67
                                          ─────
                                          $0.69/month

Under seventy cents. A t3.small that could do the same job costs about $15/month and sits idle most of the time.

The math flips when load is steady and high. A function pulling constant traffic at 200 requests/second all day is not cheaper than a couple of right-sized EC2 instances — it's often several times more expensive. Lambda's economics are built around idle time. If you have none, you're paying a premium for elasticity you aren't using.

When not to use Lambda

Being honest about this makes the rest of the advice more useful.

Long-running work. 15 minutes is a hard ceiling. Video transcoding, large ETL jobs, anything that takes an hour — use Fargate, Batch, or Step Functions to break it up.

Steady high-volume traffic. See the cost math above.

Consistent sub-50ms latency requirements. Cold starts make tail latency unpredictable. Provisioned concurrency helps but costs you the main benefit.

WebSockets and long-lived connections. API Gateway supports WebSockets with Lambda, but the model is awkward — each message is a separate invocation with no connection state, so you're storing connection IDs in DynamoDB and it stops being simple.

Heavy stateful in-memory work. If your app depends on a big warm cache, Lambda will fight you at every step.

When your team doesn't want to run a distributed system. This one's underrated. The moment you have API Gateway, four Lambdas, a queue, and a DLQ, you've got a distributed system with distributed-system failure modes — partial failures, retries, ordering, idempotency. A single boring container running a boring web framework is sometimes just the correct answer, and choosing it isn't a failure of ambition.

The short version

Lambda runs your code in response to events and bills you for the time it runs. Everything else follows from two facts: the environment is reused but temporary, and you might get invoked more than once for the same event.

Put expensive setup outside the handler. Assume anything in global scope is a cache, never storage. Raise your memory setting — it's really a CPU setting. Set timeouts deliberately at every layer. Do the minimum synchronously and push real work to async triggers. Make your handlers idempotent before you need to. Cap concurrency on anything that touches a relational database. Give the execution role exactly the permissions it needs and nothing else. Log JSON, watch p99, keep the DLQ at zero.

None of this is complicated in isolation. It's just that every single one of these will teach itself to you in production if you skip it — usually on a weekend.

system-design-02-rate-limiter-an-end-to-.html:
Modern applications can receive thousands or even millions of requests every second.

But what happens when a single user suddenly sends thousands of requests?

What happens when a malicious client starts flooding your APIs?

Or when a popular API endpoint receives far more traffic than your backend can handle?

This is where a Rate Limiter becomes essential.

A rate limiter controls how frequently a client can access a service within a given period of time. It protects backend systems from excessive traffic while helping maintain predictable performance and availability.

In this article, we will design a scalable, distributed rate limiter from scratch and gradually move from the basic idea to a production-ready architecture.

What Are We Building?

Imagine an API that allows a user to make:

100 requests per minute.

If the user sends the first 100 requests, they are accepted.

When request number 101 arrives within the same minute, the rate limiter rejects it.

The client may receive:

HTTP 429 — Too Many Requests

The basic idea is simple.

The engineering challenge is making this work when we have:

  • Millions of users

  • Thousands of API servers

  • Multiple data centers

  • Very high request volume

  • Extremely low latency requirements

  • Distributed infrastructure

That is where system design becomes interesting.

1. Why Do We Need a Rate Limiter?

There are several reasons why production systems implement rate limiting.

1. Protect Against Abuse

Without rate limiting, a malicious client could continuously send requests and consume backend resources.

For example:

Client → 1,000,000 requests
       ↓
API Servers
       ↓
Database

The database and application servers could become overloaded.

A rate limiter stops excessive requests before they reach expensive backend services.

2. Prevent Denial-of-Service Attacks

Rate limiting can help mitigate certain types of traffic flooding and application-level denial-of-service attacks.

For example:

100 requests/sec → Allowed
1000 requests/sec → Suspicious
10000 requests/sec → Blocked

It is not a complete DDoS protection mechanism, but it provides an important layer of defense.

3. Protect Expensive APIs

Some APIs are much more expensive than others.

For example:

GET /profile
GET /posts
POST /generate-report
POST /generate-ai-response

A service may allow:

Profile API:
1000 requests/minute

AI API:
20 requests/minute

Rate limiting lets us define different limits for different operations.

4. Prevent Resource Starvation

One customer should not be able to consume all available resources.

For example, suppose we have:

1000 requests/sec capacity

If one client generates:

900 requests/sec

other users may experience slow responses.

Rate limiting provides fairer resource allocation.

2. Requirements

Before designing the system, we need to define what our rate limiter should do.

Functional Requirements

The system should:

  1. Accept incoming requests.

  2. Identify the client.

  3. Determine the applicable rate-limit rule.

  4. Count or estimate the client's request rate.

  5. Allow requests within the configured limit.

  6. Reject requests exceeding the limit.

  7. Return an appropriate response to throttled clients.

  8. Support different rate-limit rules.

For example:

User A → 100 requests/minute
User B → 1000 requests/minute
IP address → 500 requests/minute
Login API → 5 requests/minute

3. Non-Functional Requirements

A production rate limiter needs more than just correctness.

Low Latency

The rate limiter sits directly in the request path.

Therefore:

Client
   ↓
Rate Limiter
   ↓
API Server

If the rate limiter itself takes 100 ms, every API request becomes slower.

The rate limiter should therefore operate with extremely low latency.

High Availability

If the rate limiter goes down, should the entire application go down?

Ideally, no.

The system should be highly available and fault tolerant.

Scalability

The system should support:

Thousands → Millions → Billions of requests

as the application grows.

Distributed Operation

In a production environment, we usually have multiple API servers.

For example:

             Load Balancer
              /    |    \
             /     |     \
          Server Server Server

The rate limiter must work correctly even when requests from the same client reach different servers.

4. Clarifying the Scope

In a system design interview, it is important to ask clarification questions before designing.

For our system, let's assume:

  • The rate limiter works on the server side.

  • Requests are coming through an API.

  • We need distributed support.

  • We need configurable rules.

  • We want low latency.

  • We want high availability.

  • Rate-limit state may need to be shared across servers.

For example:

User ID = 12345

Limit:
100 requests / minute

5. High-Level Architecture

A basic architecture looks like this:

                    Client
                      |
                      v
               Load Balancer
                      |
                      v
               Rate Limiter
                      |
             +--------+--------+
             |                 |
             v                 v
          Redis             Rule Store
             |
             v
         API Servers
             |
             v
          Database

The rate limiter becomes a layer between the client and application servers.

The request is first checked against the configured rate limit.

If the request is allowed:

Client
  ↓
Rate Limiter
  ↓
API Server
  ↓
Database

If the request exceeds the limit:

Client
  ↓
Rate Limiter
  ↓
429 Too Many Requests

The important point is that rejected requests do not consume resources in the application layer.

6. API Design

Our rate limiter does not necessarily need a public API of its own.

Instead, it can operate as middleware or as part of an API gateway.

For example:

GET /api/v1/users

The request first passes through the rate limiter.

The rate limiter determines:

Who is making the request?
Which endpoint is being accessed?
What is the applicable limit?
How many requests has the client already made?

Then it makes the decision.

7. How Do We Identify a Client?

One of the most important questions is:

What exactly are we rate limiting?

We could use:

IP Address

192.168.1.10

Useful for anonymous users.

But many users can share the same public IP.

User ID

user_id = 12345

Useful for authenticated applications.

API Key

api_key = abc123

Common in developer platforms.

Combination

We can also create rules such as:

user_id + endpoint

or:

IP + endpoint

For example:

login + IP → 5 requests/minute
API + user → 1000 requests/minute

A production system should therefore support configurable identifiers.

8. Rate Limiting Algorithms

There are several common algorithms for implementing rate limiting.

The most important ones are:

  1. Fixed Window

  2. Sliding Window

  3. Token Bucket

  4. Leaky Bucket

Let's understand them.

9. Fixed Window Counter

This is one of the simplest approaches.

Suppose the limit is:

100 requests / minute

We divide time into fixed windows.

12:00:00 → 12:00:59
12:01:00 → 12:01:59
12:02:00 → 12:02:59

For every client, we maintain a counter.

Example:

user_123
window = 12:00
count = 72

When another request arrives:

count = count + 1

If:

count <= 100

the request is allowed.

Otherwise:

429 Too Many Requests

Advantage

Very simple and memory efficient.

Problem

It has a boundary issue.

Suppose a user sends:

100 requests at 12:00:59
100 requests at 12:01:01

The user has effectively sent 200 requests within approximately two seconds.

Yet both requests fall into different windows.

This can create traffic spikes.

10. Sliding Window

A sliding window looks at the actual time range rather than fixed calendar boundaries.

For example:

100 requests
within the last 60 seconds

At any moment, we examine requests made during the previous 60 seconds.

This gives more accurate rate limiting.

However, storing every request timestamp can consume significant memory.

For example:

User
 ↓
[t1, t2, t3, t4, t5, ...]

At massive scale, this becomes expensive.

11. Token Bucket

Token Bucket is one of the most commonly discussed algorithms for production rate limiting.

Imagine a bucket containing tokens.

Suppose:

Bucket capacity = 100 tokens
Refill rate = 10 tokens/sec

Every request consumes one token.

If a token is available:

Request → Allowed

If there are no tokens:

Request → Rejected

Tokens are continuously added to the bucket until the bucket reaches its maximum capacity.

This allows controlled bursts.

For example:

Bucket capacity = 100

Current tokens = 100

100 requests → accepted

Current tokens = 0

Then tokens gradually refill:

After 1 sec → 10 tokens
After 2 sec → 20 tokens
After 3 sec → 30 tokens

This makes Token Bucket particularly useful when we want to allow short bursts while controlling the long-term request rate.

12. Leaky Bucket

The Leaky Bucket algorithm behaves differently.

Imagine requests entering a bucket:

Request
Request
Request
Request
   ↓
+---------+
| Bucket  |
+---------+
     |
     | fixed rate
     v
   Server

Requests leave the bucket at a controlled rate.

If the bucket becomes full, new requests are rejected.

This produces a more predictable outgoing request rate.

13. Which Algorithm Should We Choose?

There is no single algorithm that is best for every system.

A reasonable choice for our production design is:

Token Bucket

because it:

  • Supports bursts

  • Controls sustained traffic

  • Is relatively memory efficient

  • Can be implemented efficiently

  • Works well with distributed systems

The exact choice should depend on the application's traffic pattern and requirements.

14. Why Can't We Keep the Counter in Application Memory?

Suppose we have three API servers:

             Load Balancer
              /    |    \
             /     |     \
           S1      S2      S3

User 123 sends:

Request 1 → S1
Request 2 → S2
Request 3 → S3

If every server maintains its own counter:

S1 → user123 = 1
S2 → user123 = 1
S3 → user123 = 1

The system incorrectly thinks the user has only made one request on each server.

The actual count is:

3 requests

This is why a distributed rate limiter needs shared state.

15. Redis as the Shared Store

A common approach is to use Redis.

Our architecture becomes:

                Load Balancer
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |           |           |
          v           v           v
       Server 1    Server 2    Server 3
          \           |           /
           \          |          /
            +---------+---------+
                      |
                    Redis

Redis is useful because it provides:

  • Very fast reads and writes

  • Atomic operations

  • Expiration/TTL

  • Distributed access

  • In-memory performance

For a rate limiter, these properties are extremely useful.

16. Example Redis State

Suppose we have:

user_id = 12345
limit = 100 requests/minute

We can maintain state similar to:

rate:user:12345

with information such as:

tokens
last_refill_time

The rate limiter can then calculate how many tokens are currently available.

17. The Request Flow

Let's walk through a request.

Step 1 — Client Sends Request

POST /api/v1/orders

Step 2 — Request Reaches Rate Limiter

The rate limiter extracts the client identity:

user_id = 12345

Step 3 — Load Applicable Rule

For example:

100 requests/minute

Step 4 — Check Redis

The rate limiter retrieves the client's current rate-limit state.

tokens = 37

Step 5 — Consume Token

One token is consumed:

37 → 36

Step 6 — Forward Request

Since a token was available:

Rate Limiter
      ↓
API Server

Step 7 — If No Token Exists

If:

tokens = 0

the request is rejected.

HTTP 429 Too Many Requests

The API server never receives the request.

18. Rate Limit Response Headers

A good rate limiter should tell clients useful information.

For example:

X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 37
X-RateLimit-Retry-After: 12

These headers tell the client:

  • Maximum allowed requests

  • Remaining requests

  • How long to wait before retrying

This allows clients to implement better retry behavior.

19. Why HTTP 429?

HTTP status code:

429 Too Many Requests

is commonly used when a client exceeds the allowed request rate.

For example:

{
  "error": "rate_limit_exceeded",
  "message": "Too many requests",
  "retry_after": 12
}

The client can then wait and retry.

20. Atomicity Problem

Now we reach an important distributed systems problem.

Imagine two requests arrive at exactly the same time.

Both read:

tokens = 1

Both think a token is available.

Both consume it.

Now the system has allowed two requests even though only one token existed.

This is a race condition.

We therefore need an atomic operation.

21. Redis Atomic Operations

Instead of performing:

GET
↓
Calculate
↓
SET

as three independent operations, we need the entire rate-limit decision to happen atomically.

One common solution is a Redis Lua script.

Conceptually:

Check tokens
      ↓
Calculate refill
      ↓
If token available
      ↓
Consume token
      ↓
Return ALLOW

All of this happens atomically from the perspective of other requests.

This prevents concurrent requests from incorrectly consuming the same token.

22. Rule Management

Where do rate-limit rules come from?

We could maintain them in a configuration store.

For example:

Rule:

endpoint = /api/v1/login
identifier = IP
limit = 5
window = 60 seconds

Another rule:

endpoint = /api/v1/posts
identifier = USER
limit = 100
window = 60 seconds

The rule configuration can be stored in a database or configuration service and cached by rate limiter instances.

23. High-Level Production Architecture

Putting everything together:

                         Clients
                            |
                            v
                     CDN / Edge Layer
                            |
                            v
                      Load Balancer
                            |
                            v
                    API Gateway /
                    Rate Limiter
                            |
                  +---------+---------+
                  |                   |
                  v                   v
               Redis             Rule Cache
                  |
                  |
                  v
             API Servers
                  |
                  v
              Services
                  |
                  v
              Database

The rate limiter sits close to the edge so that rejected requests are stopped as early as possible.

24. Scaling the Rate Limiter

What happens when traffic becomes massive?

Suppose we receive:

10 million requests/sec

A single rate limiter instance is obviously insufficient.

We horizontally scale:

             Load Balancer
          /       |       \
         /        |        \
       RL1       RL2       RL3
        |         |         |
        +---------+---------+
                  |
                Redis

Each rate limiter instance is stateless.

The shared state lives in Redis.

This makes adding more rate limiter instances relatively straightforward.

25. Redis Scaling

But now Redis itself can become a bottleneck.

We can introduce:

Redis Replication

        Redis Primary
          /       \
         v         v
      Replica    Replica

For read-heavy workloads, replicas can help.

However, rate limiting often requires atomic writes, so the exact replication strategy needs careful consideration.

Redis Sharding

We can distribute rate-limit keys across multiple Redis nodes.

For example:

user_1 → Redis Shard 1
user_2 → Redis Shard 2
user_3 → Redis Shard 3

A consistent hashing or cluster mechanism can determine where each key belongs.

This allows the system to scale horizontally.

26. Multi-Region Architecture

Now imagine users across the world.

              Global Traffic
                    |
        +-----------+-----------+
        |                       |
        v                       v
      India                    US
        |                       |
     Rate Limiter           Rate Limiter
        |                       |
      Redis                   Redis

If every request from India must travel to a US Redis cluster, latency increases.

Therefore, large-scale systems may deploy rate-limiting infrastructure closer to users.

However, this introduces a difficult question:

How do we maintain globally consistent limits?

For some applications, approximate limits are acceptable.

For others, strict global limits are required.

This becomes a trade-off between:

  • Consistency

  • Latency

  • Availability

  • Complexity

27. What Happens If Redis Goes Down?

This is an important production question.

Suppose:

Rate Limiter → Redis
                  X
               DOWN

What should happen?

There are two broad strategies.

Fail Open

Allow requests when the rate limiter cannot determine the current state.

Redis unavailable
      ↓
Allow request

This improves availability but can expose the backend to excessive traffic.

Fail Closed

Reject requests when the rate limiter cannot verify the limit.

Redis unavailable
      ↓
Reject request

This protects backend resources but can make the application unavailable.

Neither choice is universally correct.

The appropriate strategy depends on the API.

For example:

Login API → potentially fail closed

Read-only public API → potentially fail open

28. Rate Limiting at Different Levels

A mature system may use multiple layers of rate limiting.

IP-Level

IP → 1000 requests/minute

User-Level

User → 500 requests/minute

API-Level

/api/login → 5 requests/minute

Global-Level

Entire service → 1 million requests/sec

These layers can work together.

29. Rate Limiting vs Throttling

These terms are often used interchangeably, but there is a useful distinction.

Rate limiting determines how many requests a client can make.

Throttling generally refers to controlling or slowing traffic once it reaches a certain threshold.

For example:

Rate Limit:
100 requests/minute

Throttling:
Process requests at 10 requests/sec

The exact terminology can vary between systems.

30. Monitoring and Observability

A production rate limiter must be observable.

Important metrics include:

Total requests
Allowed requests
Rejected requests
Requests/sec
Rate-limit violations
Redis latency
Redis errors
Decision latency
Rule lookup latency

We should also monitor:

429 response rate

If suddenly 40% of requests return 429, something may have changed.

It could indicate:

  • An attack

  • A broken client

  • Incorrect configuration

  • A traffic spike

  • An overly aggressive rate limit

31. Logging

Rate-limit decisions should also be traceable.

Example:

timestamp: 2026-08-09T10:30:22Z
user_id: 12345
endpoint: /api/v1/orders
limit: 100/min
remaining: 0
decision: REJECT

However, production systems should avoid unnecessarily logging sensitive information.

32. Handling Retry Storms

There is another subtle problem.

Suppose 10,000 clients receive:

429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 10

If all clients retry exactly after 10 seconds, we could create another traffic spike.

This is called a retry storm.

Clients should therefore use strategies such as:

Exponential Backoff
+
Jitter

For example:

Retry 1 → 1 sec
Retry 2 → 2 sec
Retry 3 → 4 sec
Retry 4 → 8 sec

with randomized jitter added to spread requests over time.

33. Security Considerations

A rate limiter itself must be protected.

Attackers may attempt to bypass limits by:

  • Rotating IP addresses

  • Creating multiple accounts

  • Using multiple API keys

  • Manipulating request headers

Therefore, the identity strategy must be carefully designed.

For authenticated applications, user-based or API-key-based limits are often more meaningful than IP-only limits.

34. What If the Rate Limiter Becomes a Single Point of Failure?

We should never depend on one rate limiter instance.

Instead:

             Load Balancer
             /     |     \
            /      |      \
          RL1     RL2     RL3

If:

RL2 → DOWN

traffic can continue through:

RL1
RL3

The rate limiter layer should therefore be horizontally scalable and redundant.

35. Final Production-Ready Design

Our final design looks like this:

                         CLIENTS
                            |
                            v
                     CDN / EDGE
                            |
                            v
                      LOAD BALANCER
                            |
             +--------------+--------------+
             |              |              |
             v              v              v
           RL-1           RL-2           RL-3
             |              |              |
             +--------------+--------------+
                            |
                            v
                     REDIS CLUSTER
                            |
                            v
                    API / SERVICES
                            |
                            v
                        DATABASE

Main Components

Load Balancer

Distributes incoming requests across rate limiter instances.

Rate Limiter

Makes the allow/reject decision.

Redis Cluster

Stores distributed rate-limit state.

Rule Store

Stores configurable rate-limit policies.

API Servers

Process only requests that have passed the rate limiter.

Monitoring

Tracks traffic, latency, rejected requests, errors, and system health.

36. Key Trade-offs

System design is not about finding one perfect architecture.

It is about understanding trade-offs.

Decision

Trade-off

Fixed Window

Understanding these trade-offs is often more important than memorizing a particular architecture.

37. Interview Discussion Checklist

If you are asked to design a rate limiter in a system design interview, a useful flow is:

Step 1

Explain trade-offs.

This structure keeps the discussion organized while leaving room for deeper exploration.

38. Key Takeaways

A rate limiter may look like a simple counter:

if requests > limit:
    reject()

But at production scale, the problem becomes much more interesting.

We need to think about:

  • Distributed state

  • Race conditions

  • Atomic operations

  • Low latency

  • High availability

  • Redis scaling

  • Rate-limiting algorithms

  • Multi-region deployments

  • Failure handling

  • Retry storms

  • Monitoring

  • Security

The core idea remains simple:

Allow traffic that the system can safely handle and stop excessive traffic before it reaches expensive backend resources.

But designing that mechanism to work reliably at millions or billions of requests requires careful distributed-system thinking.

What's Next?

This is System Design 02 in our production-ready System Design series.

We started with URL Shortener, where the focus was on mapping large URLs to compact identifiers and handling high read traffic.

With Rate Limiter, we moved one layer closer to the infrastructure that protects almost every large-scale backend system.

Next, we'll continue building systems one problem at a time and explore how individual components come together to create reliable, scalable products.

HTTP Finally Got a QUERY Method: The Missing Piece We've Been Waiting For

If you've spent any time building APIs, you've probably encountered a strange situation where everything works perfectly... but deep down, you know something feels a little wrong.

Imagine you're building an e-commerce application. A user wants to search for laptops with a price below ₹80,000, at least 16 GB of RAM, an Intel processor, a rating above 4.5, available in Bangalore, sorted by popularity, excluding refurbished products. That's a perfectly reasonable search.

As developers, our first instinct is usually to use a GET request because we're retrieving data.

So we end up with a URL that looks something like this:

GET /products?category=laptop&priceMax=80000&ram=16&processor=intel&rating=4.5&city=bangalore&sort=popularity&excludeRefurbished=true

Not too bad, right?

Now imagine product managers doing what they do best—finding one more filter that "users definitely need."
Disclaimer: My PM is great. Any resemblance to your PM is purely coincidental. 😄

"Can we search by screen size?"

"Can users filter by battery life?"

"What about multiple brands?"

"Can they choose different price ranges?"

"Oh, and let's add AI-powered relevance scoring."

Before you know it, your URL is so long it starts thinking it has a shot at a Guinness World Record. Spoiler: it doesn't. 😄

At this point, almost every backend developer quietly gives up and says,

"Let's just use POST."

The Great POST Hack

Instead of sending everything through the URL, developers started sending a JSON body.

POST /products/search
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "category": "laptop",
  "filters": {
    "price": {
      "max": 80000
    },
    "ram": 16,
    "brands": [
      "Dell",
      "Lenovo"
    ]
  }
}

Problem solved.

Or... was it?

Technically, yes.

Semantically, not really.

The job of POST is to create or change things—not to hand you data on demand. It's the chef in the kitchen, not the waiter taking your order. Let everyone do the job they were hired for.

But in this example, we're not creating anything.

We're not updating anything.

We're simply asking the server,

"Can you show me laptops matching these filters?"

It's a read operation disguised as a write operation.

It's a bit like going to a library and filling out a passport application just because you wanted to borrow a book.

You'll probably get what you need eventually, but everyone involved knows this isn't how the system was meant to work.

Why Didn't We Just Use GET with a Request Body?

This is one of those questions every backend developer asks at least once.

The HTTP specification never completely forbade request bodies with GET, but it also never defined consistent behavior for them.

Some servers accept them. Some frameworks ignore them. Some proxies strip them. Many HTTP clients don't even let you send them. That's... a lot of trust issues for one request.

So although GET technically retrieves data, sending a body with GET has never been a reliable solution.

Developers needed somewhere to put complex query data.

The only universally supported option became POST.

And that's how an entire industry ended up using POST for operations that weren't actually posting anything.

Enter HTTP QUERY

After years of developers bending HTTP semantics to solve this problem, HTTP finally introduced something that fits naturally: the QUERY method.

The name itself tells you exactly what it does.

You're asking, "What's on the menu?"
Not, "Can you cook me a new dish?"
So instead of writing:

POST /products/search

you can now write:

QUERY /products
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "category": "laptop",
  "price": {
    "min": 40000,
    "max": 80000
  },
  "brands": [
    "Dell",
    "Lenovo"
  ],
  "rating": 4.5,
  "city": "Bangalore"
}

Notice how much cleaner this feels.

The endpoint isn't pretending to create a resource.

The HTTP method clearly communicates your intention.

"I'm sending a complex query, and I expect data back."

That's exactly what QUERY was designed for.

Why This Is a Bigger Deal Than It Looks

At first glance, adding another HTTP method might seem like a small change. It's like adding one more dish to the menu of the HTTP restaurant—doesn't seem like a big deal until everyone starts ordering it.

After all, we already have GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS, and HEAD.

Do we really need another one?

Actually, yes.

One of the strengths of HTTP has always been that its methods describe the intent of a request.

When you see:

  • GET, you expect to retrieve data.

  • POST, you expect something new to be created.

  • PUT, you expect a complete update.

  • PATCH, you expect a partial update.

  • DELETE, you expect something to be removed.

These methods aren't just names—they communicate behavior.

Unfortunately, complex read operations never had a proper home.

GET couldn't reliably carry request bodies.

POST wasn't semantically correct.

QUERY fills that gap.

It's not trying to replace GET.

It's complementing it.

Simple retrievals still belong to GET.

Complex retrievals with structured request bodies belong to QUERY.

A Real-World Example

Imagine you're building an analytics dashboard.

Users can choose:

  • Multiple countries

  • Custom date ranges

  • Device types

  • Browsers

  • User segments

  • Revenue filters

  • Grouping options

  • Sorting preferences

Trying to fit all of that into a URL quickly becomes unreadable.

Instead, QUERY lets you express the request naturally.

QUERY /analytics

{
  "countries": [
    "India",
    "USA"
  ],
  "dateRange": {
    "from": "2026-01-01",
    "to": "2026-06-30"
  },
  "devices": [
    "Mobile",
    "Desktop"
  ],
  "groupBy": [
    "City",
    "Browser"
  ],
  "sort": "Revenue"
}

The request is easy to understand.

The server knows this is a read-only operation.

And future developers reading your API won't have to wonder why a POST endpoint doesn't actually create anything.

Does QUERY Make APIs Faster?

Let's clear up one misconception before Twitter does it for us.

No, QUERY doesn't make your APIs faster.

It won't magically reduce latency, make your database queries execute in half the time, or sprinkle performance fairy dust over your backend. If your endpoint takes five seconds because it's running a SELECT * on a table with 50 million rows and no indexes, QUERY isn't here to save you.

What it does improve is clarity.

When someone sees a QUERY request, they immediately know what's happening: the client is asking for data, nothing is being created, and nothing is being modified. That's surprisingly valuable because APIs aren't written only for machines—they're written for developers too. Good API design is like good variable naming; it makes intentions obvious without requiring a meeting to explain them.

What About GraphQL?

If you've worked with GraphQL, you've probably been living this reality for years.

Most GraphQL operations that simply fetch data are sent using POST. Not because GraphQL wanted to reinvent HTTP, but because GraphQL queries can become so large and expressive that stuffing them into a URL would feel like writing a novel in your browser's address bar.

This is exactly the kind of problem QUERY was designed to solve.

Instead of borrowing POST for read-only operations, HTTP now has a method whose entire job is saying, "I'm here to query data." It doesn't replace GraphQL, and it isn't trying to. It simply gives REST APIs a cleaner and more expressive way to perform complex retrieval operations.

Will Everyone Start Using QUERY Tomorrow?

Probably not.

The internet has a long memory, and it doesn't change overnight.

A new HTTP method isn't just something developers start using after reading one blog post (although I'd appreciate it if they did). Browsers, web servers, reverse proxies, API gateways, CDNs, firewalls, client libraries, and frameworks all need to understand it first. That's a lot of software to convince.

For quite some time, many applications will continue using POST for complex search endpoints simply because every piece of infrastructure already knows how to deal with it. Compatibility usually wins over elegance in production systems.

But as support spreads across the ecosystem, QUERY has a very good chance of becoming the natural choice for complex, read-only operations.

Why Developers Are Excited

The interesting thing about QUERY isn't that it's revolutionary.

It's that it feels like something HTTP should have had years ago.

Developers have spent decades building workarounds for this missing piece. We've created /search endpoints, documented that certain POST requests are actually read-only, and had the same conversation with new teammates over and over again:

"Yes... it's a POST request. No... it doesn't actually create anything. Trust me."

That's not exactly the most elegant explanation.

QUERY removes that awkwardness. The method itself communicates the intent without needing comments, documentation, or an onboarding session.

Sometimes the best improvements in technology aren't flashy new frameworks or AI-powered everything. Sometimes they're small changes that quietly eliminate a tiny source of confusion that millions of developers have simply learned to live with.

Final Thoughts

HTTP has been around for more than three decades, yet it continues to evolve in thoughtful ways.

The introduction of QUERY isn't about replacing GET, making POST obsolete, or forcing everyone to rewrite their APIs next weekend. It's simply about giving developers the right tool for a problem they've been solving with workarounds for years.

Simple resource retrieval still belongs to GET. Creating resources still belongs to POST. Updating them remains the job of PUT and PATCH, while DELETE continues doing exactly what its name promises.

And now, complex, read-only operations finally have a method that describes what they're actually doing.

It's a relatively small addition to HTTP, but one that makes APIs cleaner, more expressive, and easier to understand.

Sometimes progress doesn't come from inventing something entirely new.

Sometimes it comes from finally filling the one gap that everyone had quietly been working around all along.

And in HTTP's case, that missing piece is called QUERY.
